title: How come 3 hours on a single VHS video cassette never became the norm despite some of the later high art films near the end of the 90s and start of the early 2000s having them such as Lord of the Rings?

commenti.body: The main types of VHS tapes produced were T-120 and T-160 (the numbers represent minutes of record time in the SP mode). Any load larger than that required thinner tape and ran a higher likelihood of snapping or tangling up inside the machine.

Fear of lack of quality. Back in the old days, you could set your VCR to record on ELP, or Extra Long Play. However Hollywood noticed a perceived lack in full quality, even with EP. Standard also meant you could charge more for 2 cassettes.

Higher capacity VHS tapes probably cost more whereas film companies probably had stockpiles of older tapes and could potentially rerecord over unsold films. I'm not 100% sure as I was right at the end of the VHS lifecycle but I remember watching quite a few. Never bought any though.

Same with cassettes. The longer it is, the thinner the film gets. There’s a sweet spot where it makes financial sense and it’s also still thick enough to withstand all the tension of a kiddo fucking with your stop and ff buttons

I feel old now, this is the stuff of my childhood. It's because videotapes had a limit to their length and when you bring quality parameters into the mix, it was better to have two cassettes than one.

They may have figured out some better tech for making long tapes of higher quality, but by that time DVD was already taking over anyway. In the 1980s you could record up to 6 hours on a single tape, but it'd usually look like crap on the longest recording mode.
I used to work in Woolworths, and 180's were the absolute norm.

So the T-120 and T-160 tapes were in the US and maybe elsewhere with the NTSC format....but in Australia, the most common tapes were E-180.  That's right, in Australia we had 3 hour tapes being the norm and our recording mode was just standard play, no extended recording duration.  We also had some E-240 tapes for 4 hours too but those were not as common
I think those were PAL system tapes in Australia, where we had E-180 and E-240 tapes
Yup, in the late 90s DVDs were already on the horizon for most. I had my first DVD player on my desktop in 98, and one hooked up to my TV in 99.
For home recording, there was a long-play mode where you could record twice the length but at a lower quality, if i remember correctly. But that probably wouldn't be suitable for movie distribution.
Yeah, UK, so it was PAL
Correct, but the audio/visual quality dropped significantly and VHS isn't a great video medium to start with.

True. And even at the time VHS was considered a bad format compared to what else was possible.

But, having said that, VHS looks decent on a CRT. I watched a tape recently and was surprised how well it held up. Contrast was particularly good (which I think was something CRTs were good at). Obviously, you wouldn't shoot a movie on VHS. But a movie shot on film and released on VHS could look great, provided you're not using a modern TV.
Same issue with playing SNES, N64, and older generation video game consoles on LED or flat screens. The media isn’t optimized for those screens.

This makes me wonder if BluRay will be the last physical format. Which is ridiculously sad to think about. 

I feel like BluRay is still better quality than 4K streaming.
[removed]

I go back and forth on this.

I don't mind the look of clean pixels in most games. But it really hurts the look of others. GBA games suffer the worst - the LCD grid was really pronounced and broke the image up nicely. Without that, it can get ugly.

But I also don't usually like artificial scanlines - they can be distracting and don't really feel like the real thing.
… there has been a format beyond Blu-ray for like 7 years. Blu-ray is often better than 4K streaming, but 4K discs are the cream of the crop, and especially stunning with older films.
CRT can mask the imperfections of a VHS tape....newer screens show the imperfections.
Which format? I’m lumping in Ultra HD Blu-ray with Blu-ray.
despite the name (a brand thing), 4K Ultra HD Blu-ray is another huge format leap. Regular Blu-ray players cannot play 4k discs. 4k UHD : Blu-ray :: Blu-ray : DVD

Fuck, I need a new player!? lol

Shows you how much I’ve been streaming. I hate streaming for films now. 

Thank you for educating me, seriously.

In India, most movies were 3 hours long, and we had them on one VHS cassette each. Only the really long movies (and TV shows) were split over multiple cassettes. Blank cassettes for recording were available in 120 and 180 minute variants, and after a while the 180-minute tape became the default.

Anything is possible, but there seems to be a push to end physical media.
Streaming will never match physical media, IMO.

What a damn shame too. 

When major box office films get released are they sending physical media or sending a large file for theaters? I’ve always wondered how that works for new theatrical releases now.

I was told by the manager at my local AMC theater, they receive a thumb drive.


Now, I saw The Dark Knight Rises in Fort Worth and saw the 70mm projector up close.....it was amazing....and huge!
I had a few Godzilla movies released in extended play that were largely unwatchable due to it.

And it can even depend on the game. I think a lot of PSX games look fine on modern TV’s, but even then there are exceptions. There is an effect called dithering where the developers would make a sort of checkerboard pattern and when viewed on a CRT TV the pixels would blur together and make a sort of transparent effect. It was great for smoke or force fields. But when you view those games on a modern TV the blurring is gone and you just see the checkerboard pattern.
